title: Review --- All Four Words for The

lessons.title: Review — all four words for "the"
lessons.gloss: review — the four words for "the," complete at last, and the two plural rules that feed them

needs: your eyes, because the lesson points at something written down
notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your eyes, so it is not fully a driving lesson. You will want your eyes, because the lesson points at something written down. You can listen to all of it now and come back to the parts that need looking at once you have stopped.

segments.text: Nothing new here. Before the table: how many words does Spanish have for "the"?
Four. And you have now met every one of them separately, which is why they are allowed to appear together.

utterances: masculine. singular: el libro. plural: los libros.
feminine. singular: la casa. plural: las casas.

segments.text: English has one word here and Spanish has four, so it is easy to read this table as three extra things to carry. It is not. It is two questions you were already answering — which gender? and how many? — laid out in a grid.
The first chapter of this book taught the top row. The last two chapters taught the bottom one. Nothing in this table arrived without being built.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: the two plural rules

segments.text: And underneath the grid, one rule with a repair:
Add -s. If the word ends in a consonant and the -s would be unsayable, add -es instead.
casa becomes casas, libro becomes libros, comida becomes comidas — vowels, plain -s.
usted becomes ustedes, español becomes españoles — consonants, -es.
You held the first half from chapter one and the second half from ustedes without knowing it had a name.

segments.prompt: Give the four Spanish words for the, in the order masculine singular, feminine singular, masculine plural, feminine plural.
Say the books and then the houses.

feedback.correct: Gender picks the row, number picks the column.

segments.prompt: State the plural rule in one sentence, including what happens after a consonant.
acceptedResponses: add -s, or -es when the bare s would be unsayable
-s after a vowel and -es after a consonant

feedback.incorrect: Add -s; after a consonant add -es, because the bare -s could not be said.

segments.text: Four articles — say them. (El, la, los, las.) Two questions decide which? (Gender and number.) Next: what happens to a when there is more than one — and the answer is not what you would expect.

lessons.title: Review — the half of ir you never say out loud
lessons.gloss: the plural of a verb that is two verbs — and the one ending that still reaches the half of it you never say

segments.text: "We go." (Vamos.) "They go." (Van.)
Three plural forms, and a v in every one of them.
We. Vamos., You all. Vais., They. Van.
Now say the infinitive after them: ir. No v anywhere in it.

That gap is the whole point. The forms you speak descend from vādere, "to make one's way." The name on the dictionary entry descends from īre. Two Latin verbs, one Spanish label — so the present tense is not irregular at all. It is perfectly regular, for a verb whose own infinitive Spanish stopped saying.
So what is left of īre? Almost nothing. The infinitive ir, and one door you already know how to open.
Remember what comer did when you took its ending off and put -ida on instead:
comer becomes la comida — the eaten thing.
Do the same to ir and you get la ida — the going, the outward journey. Nobody had to teach you that word. The ending built it, and it built it on the one syllable vādere never took over.
That is worth more than either word. An ending that turns a verb into the result of the verb keeps working on stems the spoken language has abandoned.

segments.instruction: vamos, vais, van — then ir, and hear the letter go missing
segments.source: [YOU SAY: *vamos*, *vais*, *van* — then *ir*, and hear the letter go missing]

segments.instruction: la comida, la ida — one ending, two verbs
segments.source: [YOU SAY: *la comida*, *la ida* — one ending, two verbs]

feedback.correct: Both start with a letter the infinitive does not have.
The plain -ais ending, on the stem from vadere.

segments.prompt: Comer gives you la comida. What does the same ending give you from ir?

feedback.correct: La ida — and it is built on the half of the verb you never say.

segments.text: "You all go"? (Vais.) Which Latin verb do vamos, vais and van belong to? (Vādere.) And which one does la ida reach? (Īre — the half of ir that stopped being spoken.)
